title: Artificial Imitation of Intelligence: No, We Are Not 80% of the Way to AGI
summary: A car and a horse can both get you from point A to point B, but that does not mean a horse is 80% of a car. We are getting very good at imitating the outputs of intelligence, but that is not obviously the same thing as building intelligence itself. A car is a car, and a horse is a horse.
articleHtml:
Disclaimer: The opinions expressed in my writings are my own and do not represent the organizations I am affiliated with. I do not use AI to draft, write, or edit my articles. I do use AI for research assistance, occasional image generation, and final reviews.

Caution: I’m about to philosophize.

Physics was once nearly solved

At the turn of the previous century, the mood amongst some serious physicists seemed to be that physics was nearly complete. In 1894, Albert Michelson, American Nobel winning physicist, argued that the underlying principles of physics were largely established, and that the future would just be about fine-tuning it. Max Planck’s professor, in 1874, advised him not to study physics as “almost everything had been discovered”.

Then in 1900, Lord Kelvin described “two clouds” hanging over physics, places where classical theory did not quite fit observations. Those clouds became Quantum Mechanics and General Relativity, the main branches of modern physics. Turns out, no, we were nowhere near solving physics.

Ironically, when Michelson gave the previously mentioned speech, his own experiment with Edward Morley was seven years old, and would only later be explained by modern physics.

There is no reason to suspect that physicists were hubristic or short-sighted. I think they genuinely felt that way based on the knowledge they had at the time.

AGI is now “nearly solved”

Last month, in a TIME interview, OpenAI’s Chief Research Officer claimed that modern AI was roughly 80% of the way to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Big Sam Altman himself says he will have AGI by the end of the year. They’re not the only ones — most leading labs have made similar claims.

This time, though, I feel that the claims may be less genuine and intentional marketing-speak. The labs moved the AGI goalpost some years ago, and may be feeling the investor pressure to say that they are about to score in a high-stakes, potentially winner-take-all race to AGI.

OpenAI, for example, defines AGI as a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work. What an odd definition of intelligence. Define a car as “something that transports people and goods” and does a horse suddenly become 80% of a car? (You could say I’m beating a dead horse… based analogy).

The term AGI already had a reasonable, largely agreed upon definition. Researchers including Ben Goertzel, Cassio Pennachin, Shane Legg, etc. defined AGI as broadly capable intelligence of the kind humans possess. Human-like intelligence — you know, what the term “general” is supposed to imply. I’m writing this article knowing I won’t get a cent out of it — it is not economically valuable at all, but it does require some level of intelligence (even if the reader disagrees).

No, what the labs are building isn’t AGI, it’s a very good approximation of human-intelligence. What we are building today is Artificial Imitation of Intelligence (AII).

AII may produce extremely useful approximations of intelligent beings, automate enormous amounts of work, transform economies, but getting better at imitating the outputs of intelligence is not necessarily the same as building AGI. We are not 80% of the way to AGI, we are moving extremely quickly along a different path that happens to meet many of the same benchmarks.

Aeroplanes didn’t take us to the moon

To me, the idea of reaching AGI using our current techniques is like trying to get to the moon by building airplanes that can fly higher and higher (this is my version of Hubert Dreyfus’ tree-climbing analogy). Building faster, better, more efficient aircraft is a great endeavour in itself, and flying higher will certainly get you “closer” to the moon — the X-15 aircraft reached space. However, getting to the moon required the creation of the V2 rocket and its progression to the Apollo program, a whole new technology-tree. If OpenAI had built the X-15 they would claim it reached 0.1% of the way to the moon, which would be technically accurate, but obvious marketing-speak.

No. I am not making the “LLMs are stochastic parrots” argument. That argument is lazy, narrow, and too simple — the type of analogy the hosts of The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast would gobble-up.

My argument is an extrapolation of Ned Block’s old thought experiment: imagine a machine containing an impossibly large lookup table with an appropriate response to anything you might say. From the outside, it would look brilliantly intelligent, but from the inside, it’s just a cheat-sheet. My extrapolation is that, instead of a lookup table, we now have far more sophisticated function approximation engines utilizing deep neural networks — Large Language Models (colloquially called AI).

The Three Clouds hanging over LLM-based AGI

Kelvin had two clouds hanging over physics. Here are three that, I believe, hang over the idea that scaling next-token prediction gets us to AGI.

2025 Mancoridis: Researchers have tested frontier models on concepts across literary techniques, game theory, and psychological bias. They usually excel in explaining the concepts, but lag behind in applying them. When they do fail, they fail differently to human students.

2024 Vafa: Similarly, researchers have trained transformers on New York taxi journeys. Models became excellent at generating near-optimal routes, but when the models’ maps were reconstructed, they showed a different city altogether. Nonexistent roads, impossible connections, and so forth. Plus, after researchers closed 1% of roads, the accuracy dropped off significantly.

2025 Vafa: Lastly, when trained to model planetary motion well enough to predict trajectories, another model was asked to explain the underlying law. The model did not, in fact, discover gravity, despite producing the correct paths. It could predict, but it had little understanding.

One experiment that counters my argument

2026 Liu: Researchers revisited the planetary experiment with a few assumptions about how physical systems behave, and it began recovering something somewhat Newtonian. This, obviously, kills the lazy-version of my argument, but not the core of it — it wasn’t more compute or a larger context window that helped, it was the model’s starting information.

Next-token prediction against reference test cases gives models remarkably little reason to understand why the world works — simply being good enough to predict what comes next is sufficient. That is an imitation of what already exists.

Last time I encountered a closed street in downtown Toronto, I did not suddenly drive into Lake Ontario (yes, it still is, and always will be, called Lake Ontario). In fancy terms we call it graceful degradation.

Artificial Imitation of Intelligence (AII) is good

Let me say this clearly: AII is good. I use these systems every day and they have definitely increased my productivity and enjoyment of work. As of writing this, OpenAI’s limited-released GPT-6 Astra has reportedly scored 95.0% on ARC-AGI-2, with Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 reaching 90.0%. This test measures the ability of models to solve novel problems from a handful of examples, with the rules never explained. These scores are IMPRESSIVE. So impressive are frontier model metrics, in fact, that much of the cybersecurity world is in a panic.

For this reason, AII will, certainly, replace a lot of tasks. But humans are not simply task-executing meat-and-bone machines. Humans can recognize when the task itself is wrong and reframe the problem, carry lessons learned across decades, deal with ambiguity, account for emotions, deal with sparse evidence, and so on. AII can replace enormous amounts of human-work, sure, but not the human.

  • AI will automate a very large fraction of economically valuable tasks — YES. It is moot to argue against this claim.
  • We are close to building a generally intelligent machine that can replace humans — NO. I have seen little evidence of this.

Even the previously mentioned GPT-6 Astra’s performance on ARC-AGI-3 (a harder agentic AGI test) jumped from 62.7% to 99.9% when given a harness that let it remember its own full reasoning between steps — a 37 point increase due to something bolted on from the outside. Even at the frontier today, then, system-level scaffolding radically changes measurements.

Breakfast vs Billion Tokens

Humans learn from the world, whereas LLMs primarily learn from the products and traces of humans. A child sees objects fall, people interact, consequences of actions, etc. and forms an understanding, whereas an LLM gets the final output of these to approximate. It is the first part that constitutes “intelligence” in my opinion -> building and continuously revising a model of reality through participation in it.

I’m not the only one who thinks so — there are some people with bigger brains and grayer hair who do as well.

  • François Chollet’s work on skill-acquisition efficiency alludes that intelligence may be less about how much you can do than how efficiently you learn something new (incidentally, ARC-AGI-3 tests are based on this idea).
  • Judea Pearl, Rodney Brooks and Hubert Dreyfus all, in different ways, argue that prediction or symbol manipulation is not obviously equivalent to causal understanding.
  • Yann LeCun’s world-model work reflects that language alone may be too thin of a substrate for general intelligence without grounding, memory, planning and interaction.

What my children do with breakfast, LLMs learn to imitate with billions of tokens. We trained AI on civilization’s homework and then became surprised when it got good at the test.

Maybe, you may argue, there is ultimately no difference between a sufficiently good imitation of intelligence and intelligence itself in the practical world. After all, I’ve built a reasonably successful career pretending to be intelligent.

However, for true progress to AGI — show me a model that hits its own Michelson-Morley anomaly, works out that its picture of the world is wrong, invents new physics, and applies it somewhere nobody trained it to.

Until then: No, OpenAI, we are not 80% of the way to AGI. We may be 80% of the way to building something that can pass for AGI to impress investors.
